name: GameGPT
summary: Studies automated game development through multi-agent planning and code generation.
detail: Planning, review, and implementation agents break down game requirements and generate code, with a focus on hallucination and redundancy. This is an early research framework for game development agents. The linked repository contains only the paper and README; it is not a verified, ready-to-deploy product.

name: OpenGame
summary: Generates browser game projects with reusable templates and debugging skills.
detail: Turns natural-language requirements into web projects using Template Skill and Debug Skill for Canvas, Phaser, three.js, and other templates. The public CLI accepts OpenAI-compatible model endpoints; the paper also introduces GameCoder-27B. Browser execution and visual judging assess build health, usability, and intent alignment. The README still lists the standalone evaluation pipeline as forthcoming; model weights and full evaluation reproducibility are not established by the framework release alone.

name: GameDevBench
summary: Evaluates coding agents on development tasks in existing Godot projects.
detail: The repository contains 333 tasks across 2D, 3D, UI, and gameplay logic. Agents receive an existing project and a task, then produce changes that can be checked in the engine. Comparable official runs require Godot 4.4.1 and provide image or video feedback. This measures bounded development tasks, not the quality of commercial games created from scratch.

name: GameXpert-Bench
summary: Benchmarks game creation, bug fixing, and iterative improvement in three tracks.
detail: The paper introduces GameGen, GameFix, and GameOpt using complete development trajectories to study the lifecycle beyond a single generation. At review, the official repository still said data and evaluation code were being prepared for release. Treat it as a paper and protocol reference, not a ready-to-run benchmark.

name: GameGen-Verifier
summary: Verifies generated game behavior through runtime state hooks and focused checks.
detail: Breaks game requirements into independently testable checkpoints and checks functionality through browser and runtime adapters. The repository provides GGV-Harness and verifier skills for Codex and Claude. Public code does not include all generated games, run outputs, or private configurations. State hooks also provide observability beyond a purely black-box playtest.

name: MarioGPT
summary: Generates playable Mario-style level layouts from text with a GPT model.
detail: Descriptions of enemies, pipes, and elevation become character-grid levels and previews, with an interactive simulator or A* checks available. It generates level content within existing rules and supports research on controllable procedural content generation. Its scope does not include game engines, character art, or complete gameplay code.

name: GAVEL
summary: Combines language models and quality-diversity search to create board game rules.
detail: Uses Ludii game description code as its representation. A language model mutates and recombines rules, then simulation and search select games. Code, experiments, and related model and data references are public. The outputs are board games within a rule system; these results do not establish general 2D action game development ability.

name: Cardiverse
summary: Connects card game design, Python rule code, and playtesting in a prototype pipeline.
detail: Uses mechanism graphs and retrieval to generate variants and code from card game descriptions, then iteratively checks rule consistency using generated match records. The repository also includes a gameplay AI arena, but its development contribution centers on rule and code prototypes. Public substitute rule descriptions differ from the original paper inputs, which affects reproducibility.

name: Agent Game Forge
summary: A local 2D game IDE with a scene editor for Codex and Claude Code.
detail: Agents, asset workflows, and JSON scene data turn natural-language requests into JS + Canvas games. Users can adjust layout and collision in a visual editor. The README lists web output as the current default, with full Godot and Unity support still on the roadmap. The project describes itself as pre-launch.

name: Text2Game
summary: Turns long-form text into world, character, and event data for narrative prototypes.
detail: Analyzes text in chunks, merges the results, and generates Twine/Chapbook HTML or Godot visual novel projects. The repository provides a Python pipeline and examples for research on turning narratives into playable prototypes. It offers no general guarantee of generating arbitrary action games.

name: PixelLab AI Agent Toolkit
summary: Generates pixel characters, animation, and seamless tilesets through API and MCP tools.
detail: Accepts character descriptions, directions, actions, and terrain conditions to produce pixel assets, including four- or eight-direction characters and side-view or top-down tilesets. This is a commercial asset service. MCP connects its asset tools to coding agents; game rules, collision, and asset import still require a project workflow.

name: Agent Sprite Forge
summary: Combines reference art, generated animation, and deterministic processing into exportable sprites.
detail: Generates motion clips from an approved reference image, then performs background removal, alignment, loop selection, timing correction, and atlas packaging. It offers Godot, Aseprite, and web exports. For 0.4.0, the README reports parse-level round trips but no Godot, LDtk, or Aseprite editor-import verification. Import and visual acceptance checks remain necessary.

name: 3AGameFactory
summary: Coordinates game assets, gameplay, and UI through skills, model pipelines, and engine adapters.
detail: A coding agent routes requirements through image, 3D, motion, audio, and other pipelines to produce assets and engine-native code, with context for UE5, Unity, Godot, Blender, and three.js. Demos mix generated and existing resources. The 3A name is not a verified commercial quality rating. This is a separate project from Kling's GameFactory video world model.

name: GameEngineBench
summary: Tests agent-written C++ runtime changes in real Unreal Engine projects.
detail: Paper v2 describes 110 scoped C++ tasks from nine Unreal projects. Agents receive a buildable start, allowed files, and behavioral requirements. After compilation and Play-in-Editor listen-server tests, an LLM judge reviews the specification, test evidence, edits, and reference solution to determine success. The paper-linked repository could not be retrieved during review, so runnable-code availability remains unverified. The scope is local C++ implementation, not complete 3D game generation.

name: Unity Agent Plugin
summary: Unity-maintained project skills give general coding agents engine-specific context.
detail: Provides Claude Code, Codex, and Grok with skills for 2D, UI, rendering, navigation, physics, multiplayer, and other tasks, connected to Unity CLI and MCP controls. Unity requires version 6.0 or later. The current CLI MCP mode replaces MCP in the older assistant package; follow the documentation for the version in use.

name: MCP Unity Editor
summary: A community MCP bridge for querying, editing, and testing Unity projects.
detail: Exposes scenes, GameObjects, components, Prefabs, logs, Unity Test Runner, and other editor operations to MCP clients. This community tool is separate from Unity's official plugin. Its README warns that entering Play Mode with domain reload can disconnect the bridge; check the installed version, test configuration, and actual results. Editor automation alone does not establish correct gameplay.

name: Godot MCP 3D Asset Builder
summary: Builds reusable stylized 3D assets with Godot geometry and validation workflows.
detail: Takes project style and asset requirements, then uses Godot MCP and deterministic builders to produce PackedScene assets and check grounding, collision, navigation, and screenshots. Designed for Codex and Claude Code, it can reuse existing project resources. It requires compatible MCP capabilities and is not an image-to-mesh generative model.

name: Hunyuan3D 2.0
summary: Turns reference images into geometry and textures for 3D asset pipelines.
detail: The 2.0 pipeline generates shape with Hunyuan3D-DiT and textures the mesh with Hunyuan3D-Paint. It supports GLB and OBJ export and a Blender addon under a dedicated Tencent Hunyuan 3D 2.0 community license. The separate 2.1 release adds a PBR texture pipeline and training code. Topology, LOD, rigging, collision, runtime performance, and each version's terms still need game-pipeline checks.

name: TRELLIS
summary: Generates meshes, Gaussians, and radiance fields from structured latent representations.
detail: Decodes image or text inputs into several 3D representations. Official examples support textured GLB export and simplification. Conventional game asset pipelines mainly use its mesh branch; Gaussian and radiance field outputs do not themselves include usable collision, animation, or gameplay logic.

name: TripoSR
summary: Quickly reconstructs a 3D object from one image for asset prototyping.
detail: Uses LRM-style feed-forward reconstruction, with public code, pretrained models, and a demo. An input image becomes an exportable object mesh. It focuses on individual objects; hidden surfaces, topology, and game performance need additional work. It is not a complete scene or playable game generator.

name: Infinigen
summary: Procedurally generates natural and indoor Blender scenes and synthetic data.
detail: Random seeds, parameters, and asset generators produce geometry, materials, scenes, and annotations, with export documentation for OBJ, OpenUSD, and other formats. This is a procedural system rather than a language model. It can provide controllable scenes and data for AI development workflows; real-time games still need optimization, collision, and gameplay integration.

name: Holodeck
summary: Lays out and furnishes interactive 3D indoor environments from text.
detail: Combines language planning, asset retrieval, and spatial constraints to turn room requirements into AI2-THOR scenes, with instructions for loading them in Unity. Evaluation primarily targets embodied AI environment generation. It offers ideas for scene layout and semantic interaction, but does not establish complete game level design or commercial release readiness.

name: Video2Game
summary: Reconstructs real-world video into interactive 3D environments for the browser.
detail: Video and camera information pass through reconstruction, mesh extraction, appearance baking, and collision generation into a three.js game environment. The documented UE route recommends fully diffuse baked meshes, with the baking specular dimension set to zero. This is an explicit environment reconstruction approach with remaining manual scene setup and physics integration. It should be distinguished from interactive video world models that predict the next frame.

name: BlenderLLM / BlendNet / CADBench
summary: Studies text-to-Blender scripting with a training dataset and modeling benchmark.
detail: BlenderLLM generates bpy modeling scripts from user instructions. The repository and released dataset documentation report about 12K BlendNet pairs, and CADBench includes synthetic and forum-sourced tasks. Evaluation focuses on basic CAD-style modeling and instruction following. The README identifies limitations in advanced materials, multimodal input, and multi-turn collaboration; this is not a game creation benchmark.
